title: How to Read an Engineering Blog Post Critically
description: A practical checklist for separating transferable lessons from context-specific stories when reading architecture and scalability write-ups from large tech companies.
author: BlogAI Editors

toc.text: Start with the problem, not the solution
Separate the claim from the evidence
Map it to your own constraints

html:
Company engineering blogs are some of the most useful public writing about real systems. They are also written by teams with a specific scale, budget, history, and set of constraints that are rarely spelled out. Reading them well means asking which parts of the story would survive in your own environment.

Start with the problem, not the solution

Before judging the architecture, write down the problem in one sentence. A post about rebuilding a message queue makes sense only once you know whether the pain was throughput, operational cost, ordering guarantees, or team ownership.

If you cannot state the problem after reading the introduction, the post is probably describing a solution looking for a justification, and the lessons will be hard to transfer.

Find the numbers that matter

Scale changes which designs are reasonable. Look for:

  • Request or event volume, ideally with peak and average figures.
  • Data size and how fast it grows.
  • Latency targets and which percentile they refer to.
  • Team size that builds and operates the system.

When these are missing, treat performance claims as directional rather than as evidence you can plan around.

Separate the claim from the evidence

A useful habit is to keep a two-column note while reading:

The post claims The evidence shown
"Migration cut latency in half" A before/after chart, but no load figures
"The new design is simpler" Fewer services, but a new dependency
"No downtime during rollout" A described dual-write strategy

Claims with concrete evidence are the ones worth citing in your own design reviews.

Look for what went wrong

The most transferable sections are often the incidents, rollbacks, and abandoned approaches. A post that lists only successes is either very short on detail or leaving out the part you most need. Pay attention to phrases like "we initially tried" or "in hindsight": they usually introduce the real lesson.

Map it to your own constraints

Finally, check the design against what you actually have:

  1. Do you have the same failure modes, or are you solving a problem you do not have yet?
  2. Could your team operate the extra components on call?
  3. What is the smallest version of this idea that would help today?

A quick worked example

Suppose a post describes sharding a database by customer ID to handle growth. The transferable idea is partitioning by the key most queries already filter on. The non-transferable part may be the custom routing layer, which was only needed because of thousands of shards. At smaller scale, built-in partitioning in your existing database may give you the same benefit.

Further reading

The Engineering category collects blogs that publish this kind of write-up regularly. If you want them in one place, follow them with a feed reader as described in How to Follow Technical Blogs with RSS and OPML.

title: How to Follow Technical Blogs with RSS and OPML
description: Set up a feed reader, import the BlogAI OPML file, and build a reading routine that keeps you current without endless tabs or algorithmic timelines.
author: BlogAI Editors

toc.text: What RSS and OPML actually are

html:
Most of the best technical writing on the web still lives on independent blogs. Their authors publish when they have something worth saying, which is exactly why checking them by hand does not work: you visit ten sites, nine have nothing new, and you stop visiting. RSS solves this by letting the blogs come to you.

What RSS and OPML actually are

RSS (and its close relative Atom) is a small XML file a website publishes alongside its pages. Each entry lists a post's title, link, date, and usually a summary. A feed reader polls these files and shows you only what is new.

OPML is a list of feeds. It is how you move a whole set of subscriptions between readers in one step. A minimal OPML file looks like this:

<opml version="2.0">
  <head><title>My Feeds</title></head>
  <body>
    <outline text="Engineering">
      <outline type="rss" text="Example Blog"
               xmlUrl="https://example.com/feed.xml"
               htmlUrl="https://example.com" />
    </outline>
  </body>
</opml>

Each nested outline becomes a folder in most readers, so the categories in a well-made OPML file carry straight over into your reader.

Step 1: Choose a feed reader

Any reader that can import OPML will work. When comparing them, these are the features that matter for technical reading:

Feature Why it matters
OPML import and export Lets you start from a curated list and leave without lock-in
Folders or tags Keeps engineering, maths, and science feeds separate
Full-text view Long posts are easier to read without the site's layout
Keyboard shortcuts Triage fifty items in a few minutes
Sync across devices Read on the phone, save for the desk

Self-hosted readers are a good option if you already run a home server; hosted readers are simpler if you do not.

Step 2: Import the BlogAI collection

  1. Download the BlogAI OPML file. It contains every blog in the community directory that publishes a feed, grouped by category.
  2. In your reader, find the import option (usually under settings or subscriptions) and choose the downloaded file.
  3. Delete the folders you do not care about. A smaller list you actually read beats a large one you ignore.

You can also subscribe to a single blog: every listing in the directory with a feed shows an RSS button that copies or opens its feed URL.

Step 3: Build a reading routine

Feeds only help if you have a habit for clearing them:

  • Triage, then read. Skim headlines once a day and save only what is worth a full read.
  • Separate fast and slow feeds. News-style sites post daily; personal blogs post monthly. Put them in different folders so the slow, high-signal posts are not buried.
  • Mark all as read without guilt. If a folder overflows after a holiday, clear it. The important posts will be referenced again.

Troubleshooting common feed problems

The site has no feed link. Try common paths such as /feed, /rss, /feed.xml, or /atom.xml. Many readers also discover feeds automatically when you paste the site's home page URL.

The feed only shows summaries. That is the publisher's choice. Use your reader's full-text option if it has one, or open the post in the browser.

A feed stopped updating. Sites move platforms and feed URLs change. Check the site's footer for a new feed link, and if a directory listing is out of date, submit a correction.
